prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms

statement.case_for: I ranked B006 first and B046 sixth in my opening ballot, and having read the eight ballots I have moved B046 to the top of my preferred configuration. The optical lattice clock is a single, well-defined invention: Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the light-shift problem of trapping neutral atoms, and the Lamb-Dicke confinement of very many atoms then gives both accuracy and stability. Fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 have been reproduced and surpassed by independent laboratories on several continents, and clock-to-clock comparisons agree at that level. The consequences are concrete: a redefinition of the second is being prepared, relativistic geodesy has become practical, and constraints on varying constants and dark-sector couplings are now being set. Four colleagues (Kroll, Lindroth, Pearce, Olsson) place it in their top three, and they reach that view from different angles: atomic structure, laser spectroscopy and experimental instrumentation. Attribution is also the cleanest on the shortlist: a two-name prize pairing the proposer and first strontium demonstration (Katori) with the group that drove the accuracy and many-body clock work (Ye), with no forced exclusion among the credited names. Circuit QED remains for me the most consequential recent development in quantum optics, but I do not think I should be its principal advocate in this room (see conflict note).
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes. The 2005 prize (Hall and Haensch, frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, with Haroche) already honoured the optical-frequency and single-ion clock technologies that the lattice clock builds on, so a sceptic can say this is an incremental, if large, advance in precision within a recognised line. There is also the timing question Lindroth raised, whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second, and the allocation question beyond Katori and Ye (Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, the Paris and Boulder groups). I also have to be honest that I am not an expert on clock systematics, and my own opening ranking of B046 at sixth shows that I weighted quantum-information relevance more than metrological reach. I treat that as a limitation of my own vantage point and not as evidence against the candidate.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B046 first as the clearest case where a laser-spectroscopy technique has changed what can be measured, with low 1e-18 uncertainty, independent reproduction worldwide, and a two-name configuration he would not widen. He also ranks B006 seventh because the 2025 prize recognised adjacent superconducting-circuit physics.
responses.response: I agree with him on both points, and the second is the one that moved me. On B046 I accept that a two-name prize is defensible and that widening it to Lemonde, Ludlow or others would dilute a clean attribution. On B006 I disagree only in part: the 2025 prize honoured macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in a circuit, which is physically distinct from the cavity-QED architecture, and I do not think proximity makes B006 ineligible. But proximity is a legitimate argument for patience, and I cannot be the neutral judge of it, so I will not insist on B006 this year.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B046 first, stressing the atomic-structure core (polarizabilities and blackbody shifts) and the pending redefinition of the second, but asks whether Ye's role is better described as leading realisation than co-invention, and whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes cover the area.
responses.response: I take the role question seriously but would not let it split the pair. Katori supplied the concept and the first strontium lattice clock; Ye's group made the clock a record-setting instrument and developed many-body clock physics, which is a step beyond realisation. A citation phrased as 'invention and realization' reflects that division honestly. On waiting for the redefinition, I see little reason for it, because the scientific result is established regardless of the metrological decision, and the Nobel Prize has not historically waited for institutional adoption. On the earlier prizes, I think overlap is real but limited: combs and ion clocks are different enabling technologies, whereas the neutral-atom lattice is a new route to stability.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B038 first as an original, general concept (Z2 topological insulators) that reshaped condensed-matter physics, with over fifteen years of confirmation, calling recognition timely and arguably overdue even given the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I agree about the importance and I ranked it fourth myself. My qualification is attribution rather than merit. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe realisation that Molenkamp then observed, and the three-dimensional work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hsieh and Hasan lies outside the credited names. A prize that leaves out the HgTe prediction while crediting its experimental confirmation is the kind of gap we should avoid creating when we have a cleaner alternative. I would keep B038 as my second alternative and would want to hear whether a different configuration within the credited names fits the historical record better.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B042 first and B006 second, treating circuit QED as a natural but distinct successor to the 2025 topic, and chooses Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf with the experimental weight in mind, while accepting that excluding Girvin is contestable.
responses.response: We share the view that B006 is distinct from the 2025 physics, and I am glad to see it ranked highly. I differ on the trio: Girvin co-authored the 2004 proposal and developed the theory of dispersive readout and photon-mediated coupling that experiments depend on, so I would exclude Blais rather than Girvin, though I recognise Blais's contribution is also real and I do not think the choice can be resolved from the supplied record. I also gently disagree with the point that B042 should lead: the pairing mechanism is still debated and the field is younger, so I would place it below B046 on maturity.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B046 first as an unambiguous instrument-level achievement confirmed by many national laboratories, and regards B006 as mature but needing care because of its closeness to the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I agree that the lattice clock is an unambiguous experimental achievement and that independent clock comparisons agreeing at the 1e-18 level are the sort of confirmation we want. His point that B006 needs care on timing is fair, and I would add that the care includes who is arguing for it. I do not agree that B025 (Halzen) belongs ahead of the quantum-optics entries, because the source of the diffuse neutrino flux is still unidentified and a single-name award for a large collaboration is awkward, but that is outside my field and I defer to him on the astroparticle evidence.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and 2012 ion-clock prize.
Whether a Katori and Ye prize is complete without Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto or other early strontium-lattice contributors.
For B006, which three of Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff should be credited, and whether the 2025 prize makes a circuit-QED award too close in time.
For B038, whether the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang from the credited names can be accepted.
I rely on recollection of achieved clock uncertainties and have not verified the current record values from the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: A specific connection applies to B006 (circuit QED) and is relevant to the circuit-QED discussion generally. I work in circuit and waveguide QED at Chalmers, direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, have Chalmers colleagues (Per Delsing, C. M. Wilson) and a frequent co-author (Anton Frisk Kockum) in the same field, and Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. I rank B006 first in my opening ballot, so my support for it should be read with that interest in mind, and I would consider recusing myself from its decision if it is the leading candidate. I see no specific connection to B046, B038 or the other shortlisted candidates.
